guidePatch.title: Thailand: which foreign receipts must you bring home?
guidePatch.seoTitle: Thai foreign receipts: USD 10 million threshold and two 360-day clocks
guidePatch.description: Understand the Thai foreign-receipt threshold, the separate steps for bringing money home and selling or depositing it, and the conditions on overseas use.
guidePatch.learningSummary: For receipts covered by the Bank of Thailand (BOT) rule, bringing money back and later selling or depositing it with a Thai bank are separate steps. Its stated trigger is at least USD 10 million or equivalent. Eligible overseas expenses have a conditional alternative; that is not general permission to net any payment.

sections.heading: Use the Thai threshold, including its boundary
paragraphs: The Bank of Thailand’s 20 January 2026 statement describes an increase from USD 1 million to USD 10 million per transaction. The reviewed Thai summary says at least USD 10 million or equivalent. A receipt exactly at that amount should not be treated as below the trigger.

Ministry of Finance Notification 11 sets the formal threshold for goods exports. Published in the Gazette on 19 January 2026 and effective the next day, it sets a below-USD-10-million exception for goods outside its named categories, plus conditional exceptions for specified larger goods exports. The Bank’s implementing Notice 35 also replaces the foreign-currency acquisition exception with a below-USD-10-million test. A goods-specific exception still needs its own conditions; it should not be copied onto a service or royalty invoice.

The older English summary still displays USD 1 million. It is a disclosed source conflict, not the figure substituted for the reviewed Thai rule. The receipt’s category still matters: amount alone cannot classify it.

sections.heading: The summary has two clocks and a conditional overseas-use route
paragraphs: For the receipt covered by section 2.1, the BOT summary says to bring it back immediately, no later than 360 days from the export or transaction date. It separately says to sell or deposit the currency with a commercial bank in Thailand within 360 days from when it is acquired or brought in. These are different starting events; 360 days is not a general invitation to wait.

The summary permits received foreign currency to pay or offset eligible overseas expense obligations without first bringing it back. Its footnote excludes foreign securities investment and purposes requiring prior BOT permission, including foreign FX/baht trades, related baht derivatives and gold payments without import. It is not unrestricted netting.

For American support receipts used to pay a trainer, identify the full fee, withholding, separate expense and actual dates, then establish whether the proposed use fits. BOT’s current-hosted bank guideline lets banks ask for further documents or information where appropriate; a customer’s transaction purpose remains important.

sections.heading: Currency treatment does not decide tax or work permission
paragraphs: Thailand appears in the reviewed IRS income-tax index and E-1/E-2 table. Neither supplies a universal withholding rate, transaction permission or individual eligibility. Thai incorporation does not decide the worker’s treaty nationality; assess an actual American assignment separately.

guidePatch.reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source and guidance review; no professional legal review
limitations: The formal amendments address specific goods exceptions, foreign-currency acquisition and gold transactions; Notification 12’s gold rules are outside this guide. The BOT-hosted English translation has an Officer35 signature-date discrepancy. Original Thai controls and no unsupported Officer35 commencement date is supplied.

The receipt’s actual category, dates, exclusions, overseas use and bank documents still need to be applied. The two clocks come from the current Thai official summary; this is not a complete consolidated survey of every Thai FX rule or a bank approval.

fields.title: Thailand’s Thai summary and formal amendments distinguish the USD 10 million boundary
interpretationLimits: The formal January2026 source-access gap is closed for Ministry Notifications11/12 and OfficerNotice35. The Thai originals and official English translations were read; the latter’s Officer35 signature-date discrepancy is retained. No exact Officer35 Gazette commencement is inferred from the Ministry11 Gazette header.

The two-clock summary, individual receipt classification, permitted overseas uses and bank documentation remain conditional. No universal goods exception, service/IP classification, bank approval or complete consolidated-law survey is supplied.
conflicts: BOT English summary still displays USD 1 million; BOT current Thai summary and 20 January 2026 statement display USD 10 million. Current Thai guidance and dated statement are prioritised; underlying forms and exact application remain a bank/professional task.
OfficerNotice35 is signed23January2026 in the Thai original, while the BOT-hosted unofficial English translation says15January2026; the Thai original is prioritized.

unresolved: Actual receipt category, both clock-start dates, applicable exclusions, overseas-use purpose and the bank’s supporting documents still require the transaction facts.

The original Thai Officer35 signature date differs from its unofficial English translation. Its Gazette-publication date is not established by the attached Ministry11 header; no exact Officer35 commencement date is claimed.
This closes the named January formal-text gap, not every later Thai FX amendment or a complete country legal survey.
